claim: Protein synthesis ends when a ribosome reaches an mRNA stop codon.
source: Protein synthesis ends when a ribosome reaches an mRNA stop codon.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of translation termination.

claim: Release factors decode the stop codon.
source: Release factors (RFs) decode the stop codon, hydrolyze peptidyl-tRNA to release the nascent protein, and then dissociate to allow ribosome recycling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about release factor function.

claim: Release factors hydrolyze peptidyl-tRNA to release the nascent protein.
source: Release factors (RFs) decode the stop codon, hydrolyze peptidyl-tRNA to release the nascent protein, and then dissociate to allow ribosome recycling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about release factor function.

claim: Release factors dissociate to allow ribosome recycling.
source: Release factors (RFs) decode the stop codon, hydrolyze peptidyl-tRNA to release the nascent protein, and then dissociate to allow ribosome recycling.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about release factor function.

claim: Five structures of E. coli 70S•RF2 were resolved at up to 3.3 Å resolution in a single sample.
source: To visualize termination by RF2, we resolved a cryo-EM ensemble of E. coli 70S•RF2 structures at up to 3.3 Å in a single sample.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental cryo-EM data collection and structure determination.

claim: Five structures suggest a highly dynamic termination pathway.
source: Five structures suggest a highly dynamic termination pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural data obtained in the study.

claim: Upon peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis, the CCA end of deacyl-tRNA departs from the peptidyl transferase center.
source: Upon peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis, the CCA end of deacyl-tRNA departs from the peptidyl transferase center.
evidence: This observation is based on the structural data showing lack of density for the CCA end in Structure II.

claim: The catalytic GGQ loop of RF2 is rearranged into a long β-hairpin that plugs the peptide tunnel.
source: The catalytic GGQ loop of RF2 is rearranged into a long β-hairpin that plugs the peptide tunnel, biasing a nascent protein toward the ribosome exit.
evidence: This structural observation is directly supported by cryo-EM density in Structure II.

claim: The β-hairpin conformation of the GGQ loop biases a nascent protein toward the ribosome exit.
source: The catalytic GGQ loop of RF2 is rearranged into a long β-hairpin that plugs the peptide tunnel, biasing a nascent protein toward the ribosome exit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation that the β-hairpin blocks the peptide tunnel.

claim: Ribosomal intersubunit rotation destabilizes the catalytic RF2 domain on the 50S subunit.
source: Ribosomal intersubunit rotation destabilizes the catalytic RF2 domain on the 50S subunit and disassembles the central intersubunit bridge B2a, resulting in RF2 departure.
evidence: This is based on structural observations showing reduced density for the catalytic domain in Structure IV.

claim: Ribosomal intersubunit rotation disassembles the central intersubunit bridge B2a.
source: Ribosomal intersubunit rotation destabilizes the catalytic RF2 domain on the 50S subunit and disassembles the central intersubunit bridge B2a, resulting in RF2 departure.
evidence: This is directly observed in Structure V where H69 is disengaged from the decoding center.

claim: Disassembly of bridge B2a results in RF2 departure.
source: Ribosomal intersubunit rotation destabilizes the catalytic RF2 domain on the 50S subunit and disassembles the central intersubunit bridge B2a, resulting in RF2 departure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Structure V lacks RF2 and has a disassembled B2a bridge.

claim: Ribosomes terminate translation when release factors recognize an mRNA stop codon in the A site.
source: Ribosomes terminate translation when release factors (RFs) recognize an mRNA stop codon in the A (aminoacyl-tRNA) site (Brenner et al., 1967; Brenner et al., 1965).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from Brenner et al.

claim: Upon stop-codon recognition, the release factor hydrolyzes peptidyl-tRNA in the P site of the large subunit.
source: Upon stop-codon recognition, the release factor hydrolyzes peptidyl-tRNA in the P site of the large subunit, thus releasing nascent protein from the ribosome (Capecchi, 1967a; Capecchi, 1967b; Scolnick et al., 1968; Tompkins et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the 1960s-1970s literature.

claim: In bacteria, RF1 recognizes UAA or UAG codons.
source: In bacteria, RF1 recognizes UAA or UAG, and RF2 recognizes UAA or UGA codons (Nakamura et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 1995.

claim: In bacteria, RF2 recognizes UAA or UGA codons.
source: In bacteria, RF1 recognizes UAA or UAG, and RF2 recognizes UAA or UGA codons (Nakamura et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 1995.

claim: Following peptide release, RF1 or RF2 must dissociate from the ribosome to allow the ribosome and release factor to recycle.
source: Following peptide release, RF1 or RF2 must dissociate from the ribosome to allow the ribosome and release factor to recycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the termination cycle.

claim: Recent biophysical and biochemical findings suggest a highly dynamic series of termination events.
source: While structural studies have provided snapshots of some peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis steps (reviewed in Dunkle and Cate, 2010; Korostelev, 2011; Ramakrishnan, 2011; Rodnina, 2018; Youngman et al., 2008), recent biophysical and biochemical findings suggest a highly dynamic series of termination events (Adio et al., 2018; Indrisiunaite et al., 2015; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009), which have not been structurally visualized.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent biophysical and biochemical studies.

claim: The highly dynamic series of termination events have not been structurally visualized prior to this study.
source: While structural studies have provided snapshots of some peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis steps (reviewed in Dunkle and Cate, 2010; Korostelev, 2011; Ramakrishnan, 2011; Rodnina, 2018; Youngman et al., 2008), recent biophysical and biochemical findings suggest a highly dynamic series of termination events (Adio et al., 2018; Indrisiunaite et al., 2015; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009), which have not been structurally visualized.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction to motivate the current study.

claim: In the pre-termination state, the substrate peptidyl-tRNA resides in a non-rotated conformation of 70S ribosome.
source: In the pre-termination (pre-hydrolysis) state, the substrate peptidyl-tRNA resides in a non-rotated (classical) conformation of 70S ribosome, with its anticodon stem loop bound to the mRNA codon in the P site of the small 30S subunit and the 3′-terminal CCA-peptidyl moiety in the P site of the large 50S subunit (Agrawal et al., 2000; Ermolenko et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Agrawal et al., 2000 and Ermolenko et al., 2007.

claim: Cryo-EM and X-ray studies reveal RF1 or RF2 bound in the A site next to P tRNA.
source: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and X-ray studies reveal RF1 or RF2 bound in the A site next to P tRNA (Klaholz et al., 2003; Petry et al., 2005; Rawat et al., 2006; Rawat et al., 2003), and provide insight into pre-hydrolysis (Jin et al., 2010) and post-hydrolysis states (Korostelev et al., 2008; Korostelev et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: The release factor's codon-recognition domain (domain 2) binds the stop codon in the 30S decoding center.
source: The release factor's codon-recognition domain (domain 2) binds the stop codon in the 30S decoding center.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: The catalytic GGQ motif of domain 3 inserts into the 50S peptidyl-transferase center adjacent to the CCA end of P-tRNA.
source: The catalytic GGQ motif (glycine-glycine-glutamine of domain 3) inserts into the 50S peptidyl-transferase center (PTC) adjacent to the CCA end of P-tRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: Ribosomes retain the non-rotated conformation in RF-bound structures.
source: Ribosomes retain the non-rotated conformation in RF-bound structures, including those with mutated or post-translationally modified RFs (Pierson et al., 2016; Santos et al., 2013; Zeng and Jin, 2018) or when RFs are perturbed by the termination inhibitor blasticidin S (Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a; Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018b) or by a sense codon in the A site (Svidritskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The catalytic GGQ loop adopts the same compact conformation comprising a short α-helix in pre-hydrolysis-like and post-hydrolysis structures.
source: The catalytic GGQ loop adopts the same compact conformation comprising a short α-helix in pre-hydrolysis-like and post-hydrolysis structures, as discussed below.
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies and is contrasted with the new findings in this manuscript.

claim: In E. coli, RF1 dissociation is assisted by the non-essential GTPase RF3.
source: In E. coli, RF1 dissociation is assisted by the non-essential GTPase RF3 (Freistroffer et al., 1997; Koutmou et al., 2014), whereas RF2 can spontaneously dissociate from the ribosome (Adio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Freistroffer et al., 1997 and Koutmou et al., 2014.

claim: RF2 can spontaneously dissociate from the ribosome.
source: In E. coli, RF1 dissociation is assisted by the non-essential GTPase RF3 (Freistroffer et al., 1997; Koutmou et al., 2014), whereas RF2 can spontaneously dissociate from the ribosome (Adio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adio et al., 2018.

claim: RF3 induces rotation of the small subunit relative to the large subunit by ~9 degrees in the absence of RF1 and RF2.
source: RF3 induces rotation of the small subunit relative to the large subunit by ~9 degrees in the absence of RF1 and RF2 (Ermolenko et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2012) and stabilizes a 'hybrid' state of deacylated tRNA (P/E) (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ermolenko et al., 2007 and Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: RF3 stabilizes a 'hybrid' state of deacylated tRNA (P/E).
source: RF3 induces rotation of the small subunit relative to the large subunit by ~9 degrees in the absence of RF1 and RF2 (Ermolenko et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2012) and stabilizes a 'hybrid' state of deacylated tRNA (P/E) (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2007 and Jin et al., 2011.

claim: In the P/E conformation, the anticodon stem loop remains in the 30S P site, while the elbow and acceptor arm bind the L1 stalk and E site of the 50S subunit.
source: In the P/E conformation, the anticodon stem loop remains in the 30SS P site, while the elbow and acceptor arm bind the L1 stalk and E (exit) site of the 50S subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the P/E hybrid state of tRNA.

claim: A recent cryo-EM study showed that if RF1 is locked on the post-hydrolysis ribosome by antibacterial peptide apidaecin 137, the ribosome can undergo intersubunit rotation in the presence of both RF1 and RF3.
source: A recent cryo-EM study (Graf et al., 2018) showed that if RF1 is locked on the post-hydrolysis ribosome by antibacterial peptide apidaecin 137 (Florin et al., 2017), the ribosome can undergo intersubunit rotation in the presence of both RF1 and RF3.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Graf et al., 2018 and Florin et al., 2017.

claim: Locking RF1 on the ribosome by inactivating its catalytic motif (GGQ->GAQ) prevented RF1 recycling by RF3 from the pre-hydrolysis ribosome.
source: By contrast, biochemical experiments showed that locking RF1 on the ribosome by inactivating its catalytic motif (GGQ->GAQ) prevented RF1 recycling by RF3 from the pre-hydrolysis ribosome (Koutmou et al., 2014), echoing the deficiency of mutant RF2 (GGQ->GAQ) in stimulating GTP hydrolysis by RF3 (Zavialov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koutmou et al., 2014.

claim: Mutant RF2 (GGQ->GAQ) is deficient in stimulating GTP hydrolysis by RF3.
source: By contrast, biochemical experiments showed that locking RF1 on the ribosome by inactivating its catalytic motif (GGQ->GAQ) prevented RF1 recycling by RF3 from the pre-hydrolysis ribosome (Koutmou et al., 2014), echoing the deficiency of mutant RF2 (GGQ->GAQ) in stimulating GTP hydrolysis by RF3 (Zavialov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zavialov et al., 2002.

claim: Peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis is critical for RF dissociation.
source: These and other (Adio et al., 2018) observations indicate that peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis is critical for RF dissociation, likely due to propensity of deacylated tRNA for exiting the P site and sampling the P/E hybrid state (Moazed and Noller, 1989) via spontaneous intersubunit rotation (Cornish et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from multiple cited studies including Adio et al., 2018, Moazed and Noller, 1989, and Cornish et al., 2008.

claim: RF3 is dispensable for growth of Escherichia coli.
source: Nevertheless, RF3 is dispensable for growth of Escherichia coli (Grentzmann et al., 1994; Mikuni et al., 1994), and its expression is not conserved in bacteria (Leipe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grentzmann et al., 1994 and Mikuni et al., 1994.

claim: RF3 expression is not conserved in bacteria.
source: Nevertheless, RF3 is dispensable for growth of Escherichia coli (Grentzmann et al., 1994; Mikuni et al., 1994), and its expression is not conserved in bacteria (Leipe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leipe et al., 2002.

claim: RF3 is not present in the thermophilic model organisms of the Thermus and Thermatoga genera.
source: For example, RF3 is not present in the thermophilic model organisms of the Thermus and Thermatoga genera and in infectious Chlamydiales and Spirochaetae.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the distribution of RF3 in bacteria.

claim: RF3 is not present in infectious Chlamydiales and Spirochaetae.
source: For example, RF3 is not present in the thermophilic model organisms of the Thermus and Thermatoga genera and in infectious Chlamydiales and Spirochaetae.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the distribution of RF3 in bacteria.

claim: Both RF1 and RF2 are capable of performing a complete round of termination independently of RF3.
source: This means that both RF1 and RF2 are capable of performing a complete round of termination independently of RF3.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RF3 is not conserved in all bacteria.

claim: FRET studies demonstrate spontaneous RF1 and RF2 dissociation after peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis.
source: Indeed, recent Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) studies demonstrate spontaneous RF1 and RF2 dissociation after peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis (Prabhakar et al., 2017), coupled with transient RF sampling of the rotated ribosomes (Adio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prabhakar et al., 2017 and Adio et al., 2018.

claim: RF dissociation is coupled with transient RF sampling of the rotated ribosomes.
source: Indeed, recent Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) studies demonstrate spontaneous RF1 and RF2 dissociation after peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis (Prabhakar et al., 2017), coupled with transient RF sampling of the rotated ribosomes (Adio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adio et al., 2018.

claim: The structural basis for RF dissociation remains incompletely understood because RFs have not been structurally visualized on ribosomes with rearranged/rotated subunits in the absence of RF3 and inhibitors.
source: The structural basis for RF dissociation, however, remains incompletely understood because RFs have not been structurally visualized on ribosomes with rearranged/rotated subunits in the absence of RF3 and inhibitors.
evidence: This statement motivates the current study by identifying a gap in structural knowledge.

claim: Ensemble cryo-EM with 3D maximum likelihood classification was used to visualize the structural dynamics of RF2 on the 70S ribosome.
source: In this work, we used ensemble cryo-EM, as described earlier (Abeyrathne et al., 2016; Loveland et al., 2017), employing 3D maximum likelihood classification/sorting of particle images (Lyumkis et al., 2013; Scheres, 2010; Scheres et al., 2007) to visualize the structural dynamics of RF2 on the 70S ribosome (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The structures capture RF2 and tRNA in distinct 70S conformational states.
source: The structures capture RF2 and tRNA in distinct 70S conformational states (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structures reveal an unexpected rearrangement of the catalytic GGQ loop.
source: They reveal an unexpected rearrangement of the catalytic GGQ loop, which suggests that RF2 helps direct nascent protein out of the ribosome.
evidence: This is based on the structural observation in Structure II showing the β-hairpin conformation.

claim: The rearrangement of the catalytic GGQ loop suggests that RF2 helps direct nascent protein out of the ribosome.
source: They reveal an unexpected rearrangement of the catalytic GGQ loop, which suggests that RF2 helps direct nascent protein out of the ribosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the β-hairpin plugs the peptide tunnel.

claim: The findings reconcile biophysical observations.
source: Our findings reconcile biophysical observations and, together with other structural studies, allow a reconstruction of the termination course by RF2, from initial binding to dissociation.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings in relation to previous biophysical studies.

claim: The findings allow a reconstruction of the termination course by RF2, from initial binding to dissociation.
source: Our findings reconcile biophysical observations and, together with other structural studies, allow a reconstruction of the termination course by RF2, from initial binding to dissociation.
evidence: This is based on the ensemble of structures obtained in this study.

claim: A termination complex was formed using E. coli 70S ribosomes and RF2 to catalyze the hydrolysis of substrate N-formyl-methionyl-tRNAfMet.
source: We formed a termination complex using E. coli 70S ribosomes and RF2 to catalyze the hydrolysis of substrate N-formyl-methionyl-tRNAfMet (fMet-tRNAfMet) bound to mRNA carrying an AUG codon in the P site and a UGA stop codon in the A site.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for the study.

claim: Model termination complexes with a stop codon immediately after the start codon have been successfully used in numerous structural, biochemical and biophysical studies.
source: Although the stop codon is placed immediately after the start codon, unlike in cellular mRNAs, such model termination complexes have been successfully used in numerous structural, biochemical and biophysical studies (Adio et al., 2018; Casy et al., 2018; Koutmou et al., 2014; Kuhlenkoetter et al., 2011; Laurberg et al., 2008; Pallesen et al., 2013; Pierson et al., 2016; Shi and Joseph, 2016; Sternberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies using similar model systems.

claim: Under the conditions used for cryo-EM sample preparation, RF2 supports hydrolysis of fMet-tRNAfMet and release of fMet.
source: Indeed, under the conditions used for cryo-EM sample preparation in this work, RF2 supports hydrolysis of fMet-tRNAfMet and release of fMet (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), demonstrating activity of the ribosome and RF2 in our sample.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Maximum-likelihood classification of cryo-EM data in FREALIGN yielded five structures at average resolutions of 3.3 Å to 4.4 Å.
source: Maximum-likelihood classification of cryo-EM data in FREALIGN (Lyumkis et al., 2013) yielded five structures at average resolutions of 3.3 Å to 4.4 Å (Table 2; Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the results of the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel).
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the five structures.

claim: Structure I represents pre-termination stage with no RF2.
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Structure I based on its features.

claim: Structure II represents peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2.
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Structure II based on its features.

claim: Structure III represents tRNA exit from the PTC.
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Structure III based on its features.

claim: Structure IV represents destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2.
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Structure IV based on its features.

claim: Structure V represents post-termination stage after RF2 dissociates.
source: The structures differ by the degrees of intersubunit rotation and 30S head rotation (swivel), and are consistent with the following termination stages: pre-termination (i.e., no RF2; Structure I); peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis by RF2 (Structure II); tRNA exit from the PTC (Structure III); destabilization of the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV); and post-termination (i.e., after RF2 dissociates; Structure V).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Structure V based on its features.

claim: Structure I contains tRNA in the P site with its 3′-CCA end positioned in the peptidyl transferase center.
source: Pre-termination-like Structure I contains tRNA in the P site with its 3′-CCA end positioned in the peptidyl transferase center (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The tRNA in Structure I is likely partially or completely deacylated due to the action of RF2.
source: Although the tRNA is likely partially or completely deacylated due to the action of RF2, the tRNA and ribosome conformations closely resemble those in pre-termination aminoacyl- and peptidyl-tRNA complexes (Adio et al., 2018; Cornish et al., 2008; Jin et al., 2010; Polikanov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of RF2 in the sample and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The 30S subunit in Structure I adopts a conformation similar to crystal structures of non-rotated ribosomes with or without RFs.
source: The 30S subunit adopts a conformation similar to crystal structures of non-rotated ribosomes with or without RFs (Jin et al., 2010; Korostelev et al., 2008; Korostelev et al., 2006; Korostelev et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008; Selmer et al., 2006; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008), and exhibits a slight ~1.5° rotation relative to the 70S•RF2 crystal structure formed with the UGA stop codon (Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on comparison with multiple cited crystal structures.

claim: RF2 is bound in Structures II to IV.
source: RF2 is bound in Structures II to IV (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The 70S intersubunit rotation ranges from ~1.5° in Structure II to ~7.5° in Structure IV.
source: The 70S intersubunit rotation ranges from ~1.5° in Structure II to ~7.5° in Structure IV (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and measurements reported in Table 1.

claim: The range of rotation observed is typical of translocation complexes with tRNA.
source: This nearly full range of rotation is typical of translocation complexes with tRNA (Agirrezabala et al., 2008; Agirrezabala et al., 2012; Dunkle et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2010; Julián et al., 2008) and elongation factor G (EF-G) (Brilot et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Gao et al., 2009; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Structure II at 3.3 Å resolution accounts for the largest population of RF2-bound ribosome particles in the sample.
source: The most well-resolved 3.3 Å resolution Structure II (Figure 1B) accounts for the largest population of RF2-bound ribosome particles in the sample (Table 2), consistent with stabilization of the non-rotated 30S states by RF2 observed in FRET studies (Casy et al., 2018; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on the number of particles in the class as reported in Table 2.

claim: The large population of Structure II is consistent with stabilization of the non-rotated 30S states by RF2 observed in FRET studies.
source: The most well-resolved 3.3 Å resolution Structure II (Figure 1B) accounts for the largest population of RF2-bound ribosome particles in the sample (Table 2), consistent with stabilization of the non-rotated 30S states by RF2 observed in FRET studies (Casy et al., 2018; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural data with previous FRET studies.

claim: The overall extended conformation of RF2 in Structure II resembles that seen in published 70S•RF2 structures.
source: The overall extended conformation of RF2 resembles that seen in published 70S•RF2 structures (Korostelev et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008) with its codon-recognition superdomain (domains 2 and 4; Figure 1B) bound to the UGA stop codon in the decoding center of the 30S subunit and its catalytic domain 3 inserted into the peptidyl-transferase center.
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited published structures.

claim: Structure II features RF2 with a dramatically rearranged catalytic loop.
source: Structure II features RF2 with a dramatically rearranged catalytic loop, coinciding with the lack of density for the CCA end of the P tRNA.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Structure II shows lack of density for the CCA end of the P tRNA.
source: Structure II features RF2 with a dramatically rearranged catalytic loop, coinciding with the lack of density for the CCA end of the P tRNA.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: In previous structures, the P-tRNA CCA end binds the PTC, and RF2 forms a compact catalytic loop.
source: In previous pre- and post-hydrolysis-like structures, the P-tRNA CCA end binds the PTC, and RF2 forms a compact catalytic loop (residues 245–258).
evidence: This is based on previous structural studies.

claim: In previous structures, the catalytic 250GGQ252 motif resides at the tip of a short α-helix, adjacent to the terminal tRNA nucleotide A76.
source: In these previous structures, the catalytic 250GGQ252 motif resides at the tip of a short α-helix, adjacent to the terminal tRNA nucleotide A76 (Figure 2A, light shades; (Jin et al., 2010; Korostelev et al., 2008; Laurberg et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on multiple cited previous structures.

claim: The α-helical region of the GGQ loop is held in place by A2602 of 23S rRNA.
source: The α-helical region is held in place by A2602 of 23S ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which is critical for termination efficiency (Amort et al., 2007; Polacek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on previous structural and functional studies.

claim: A2602 of 23S rRNA is critical for termination efficiency.
source: The α-helical region is held in place by A2602 of 23S ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which is critical for termination efficiency (Amort et al., 2007; Polacek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Amort et al., 2007 and Polacek et al., 2003.

claim: In Structure II, the catalytic loop adopts an extended β-hairpin conformation that reaches ~10 Å deeper into the peptide tunnel.
source: In Structure II, however, the catalytic loop adopts an extended β-hairpin conformation that reaches ~10 Å deeper into the peptide tunnel (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and measured.

claim: To accommodate the extended β-hairpin, nucleotides G2505 and U2506 of 23S rRNA are shifted to widen the PTC.
source: To accommodate the extended β-hairpin, nucleotides G2505 and U2506 of 23S rRNA are shifted to widen the PTC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The center of the β-hairpin occupies the position normally held by A76 of P tRNA.
source: The center of the β-hairpin occupies the position normally held by A76 of P tRNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing Structure II with previous structures.

claim: The lack of density for the CCA moiety suggests that the 3′ end of P tRNA is at least partially released from the PTC.
source: The lack of density for the CCA moiety thus suggests that the 3′ end of P tRNA is at least partially released from the PTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Formation of the β-hairpin and release of the CCA moiety is accompanied by a slight shift in the P-tRNA acceptor arm away from the PTC.
source: Indeed, formation of the β-hairpin and release of the CCA moiety is accompanied by a slight shift in the P-tRNA acceptor arm away from the PTC and by ~160° rotation of nucleotide A2602 to form a Hoogsteen base pair with C1965 at helix 71 of 23S rRNA (Figure 2A and Figure 2Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Formation of the β-hairpin is accompanied by ~160° rotation of nucleotide A2602 to form a Hoogsteen base pair with C1965 at helix 71 of 23S rRNA.
source: Indeed, formation of the β-hairpin and release of the CCA moiety is accompanied by a slight shift in the P-tRNA acceptor arm away from the PTC and by ~160° rotation of nucleotide A2602 to form a Hoogsteen base pair with C1965 at helix 71 of 23S rRNA (Figure 2A and Figure 2Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The cryo-EM map shows strong density for the extended β strands.
source: The cryo-EM map shows strong density for the extended β strands (Figure 2C), but weaker density for the GGQ residues at the tip of the hairpin, consistent with conformational heterogeneity of the flexible glycine backbone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The cryo-EM map shows weaker density for the GGQ residues at the tip of the hairpin, consistent with conformational heterogeneity of the flexible glycine backbone.
source: The cryo-EM map shows strong density for the extended β strands (Figure 2C), but weaker density for the GGQ residues at the tip of the hairpin, consistent with conformational heterogeneity of the flexible glycine backbone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density and interpreted based on the known flexibility of glycine residues.

claim: The tip of the β-hairpin plugs the narrowest region of the peptide tunnel at A2062 of 23S rRNA.
source: Nevertheless, the tip of the β-hairpin plugs the narrowest region of the peptide tunnel at A2062 of 23S rRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Structure II appears to represent a previously unseen post-peptide-release state with deacyl-tRNA dissociating from the PTC.
source: Thus, Structure II appears to represent a previously unseen post-peptide-release state with deacyl-tRNA dissociating from the PTC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural features observed in Structure II.

claim: In Structure III, a 5° rotation of the 30S subunit shifts the tRNA elbow by ~10 Å along protein L5 toward the E site.
source: In Structure III (Figure 1C), a 5° rotation of the 30S subunit shifts the tRNA elbow by ~10 Å along protein L5 toward the E site.
evidence: This is directly observed and measured in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In Structure III, the P-tRNA acceptor arm pulls further out of the 50S P site.
source: As a result, the P-tRNA acceptor arm pulls further out of the 50S P site, and the end of the acceptor arm helix points at helix α7 of RF2 near positively charged Lys 282 and Lys 289.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In Structure III, the CCA moiety remains unresolved.
source: The CCA moiety remains unresolved.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: In Structure III, the 5° intersubunit rotation causes a slight 2° rotation of RF2 domain 3 relative to domain 2.
source: The 5° intersubunit rotation also causes a slight 2° rotation of RF2 domain 3 relative to domain 2, but the overall conformation of RF2 remains similar to that in Structure II, with the tip of the extended β-hairpin plugging the peptide exit tunnel.
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In Structure III, the overall conformation of RF2 remains similar to that in Structure II, with the tip of the extended β-hairpin plugging the peptide exit tunnel.
source: The 5° intersubunit rotation also causes a slight 2° rotation of RF2 domain 3 relative to domain 2, but the overall conformation of RF2 remains similar to that in Structure II, with the tip of the extended β-hairpin plugging the peptide exit tunnel.
evidence: This is observed by comparing Structures II and III.

claim: In Structure IV, the 30S subunit is rotated 7.5°.
source: In Structure IV, the 30S subunit is rotated 7.5° and the P-tRNA elbow is bound to the L1 stalk, an interaction normally observed with the P/E or E tRNA (Dunkle et al., 2011; Korostelev et al., 2006; Selmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In Structure IV, the P-tRNA elbow is bound to the L1 stalk.
source: In Structure IV, the 30S subunit is rotated 7.5° and the P-tRNA elbow is bound to the L1 stalk, an interaction normally observed with the P/E or E tRNA (Dunkle et al., 2011; Korostelev et al., 2006; Selmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In Structure IV, unlike P/E tRNA, the acceptor arm is oriented between the 50S P and E sites.
source: Unlike P/E tRNA, however, the acceptor arm is oriented between the 50S P and E sites (Figure 1D), suggesting that the tRNA adopts a transient state on its way toward the hybrid P/E conformation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The tRNA in Structure IV adopts a transient state on its way toward the hybrid P/E conformation.
source: Unlike P/E tRNA, however, the acceptor arm is oriented between the 50S P and E sites (Figure 1D), suggesting that the tRNA adopts a transient state on its way toward the hybrid P/E conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the intermediate position of the tRNA acceptor arm.

claim: The transition in Structure IV coincides with an ~3° rotation (swivel) of the 30S head.
source: This transition coincides with an ~3° rotation (swivel) of the 30S head, characteristic of intermediate stages of tRNA and mRNA translocation (Abeyrathne et al., 2016; Ratje et al., 2010).
evidence: This is measured from the cryo-EM structure and compared with previous studies.

claim: In Structure IV, the codon-recognition superdomain of RF2 moves with the 30S subunit, causing the catalytic domain to shift by ~5 Å from its position in Structure II.
source: The codon-recognition superdomain of RF2 in its canonical conformation moves with the 30S subunit, causing the catalytic domain to shift by ~5 Å from its position in Structure II (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is measured by comparing Structures II and IV.

claim: In Structure IV, reduced density for the catalytic domain and domain 1 suggests that intersubunit rotation has destabilized RF2.
source: Indeed, reduced density for the catalytic domain and domain 1, which bridges the 30S and 50S subunits at the A site periphery (Figure 1B), suggests that intersubunit rotation has destabilized RF2.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced density observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: In Structure IV, RF2 appears to be poised for dissociation and collapsing toward the compact conformation adopted by free RFs.
source: In Structure IV, therefore, RF2 appears to be poised for dissociation and collapsing toward the compact conformation adopted by free RFs (Figure 3A) (JCSG, 2005; Shin et al., 2004; Vestergaard et al., 2001; Zoldák et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features and comparison with structures of free RF2.

claim: Structure V is incompatible with RF2 binding.
source: Structure V is incompatible with RF2 binding and provides further insights into RF2 dissociation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of Structure V.

claim: Structure V provides further insights into RF2 dissociation.
source: Structure V is incompatible with RF2 binding and provides further insights into RF2 dissociation.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of Structure V.

claim: The rotated 70S•tRNA structure in Structure V resembles hybrid P/E states.
source: The rotated 70S•tRNA structure resembles hybrid P/E states, with the acceptor arm of tRNA directed toward the E site of 50S (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is observed by comparing Structure V with known P/E hybrid states.

claim: In Structure V, the central intersubunit bridge B2a is disassembled.
source: However, the central intersubunit bridge B2a—formed by helix 69 (H69, nt. 1906–1924) of 23S rRNA—is disassembled (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In RF-bound structures, the tip of H69 locks into the decoding center in a termination-specific arrangement.
source: In RF-bound structures (including Structures I to IV, above), the tip of H69 (at nt 1913) locks into the decoding center in a termination-specific arrangement (Korostelev et al., 2008; Korostelev et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008; Weixlbaumer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on observations in the current structures and previous studies.

claim: H69 interacts with the switch loop of RFs.
source: H69 interacts with the switch loop of RFs, where the codon-recognition superdomain connects to catalytic domain 3 (e.g., Structure II, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in Structure II.

claim: The interaction between H69 and the switch loop directs the catalytic domain toward the PTC.
source: This interaction directs the catalytic domain toward the PTC (Korostelev et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008) and thus defines the efficiency and accuracy of release factors (Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction between H69 and the switch loop defines the efficiency and accuracy of release factors.
source: This interaction directs the catalytic domain toward the PTC (Korostelev et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008) and thus defines the efficiency and accuracy of release factors (Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a.

claim: In Structure V, H69 is disengaged from the decoding center and moved ~15 Å toward the large subunit to pack against H71 near A2602.
source: In Structure V, however, H69 is disengaged from the decoding center and moved ~15 Å toward the large subunit to pack against H71 near A2602 (nt 1945–1961; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed and measured in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The new position of H69 in Structure V would clash with extended or compact conformations of RF2, if the release factor had remained bound to the decoding center.
source: The new position of H69 would clash with extended or compact conformations of RF2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), if the release factor had remained bound to the decoding center.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Release of RF2 appears to be coupled to rotation (swivel) of the 30S head domain.
source: Release of RF2 also appears to be coupled to rotation (swivel) of the 30S head domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations in Structure V.

claim: In RF2-bound structures, the conserved codon-recognition 205SPF207 motif of RF2 interacts with the stop codon and the 30S head near bulged nucleotide C1054 of 16S rRNA.
source: In RF2-bound structures, the conserved codon-recognition 205SPF207 motif (serine-proline-phenylalanine of domain 2) of RF2 interacts with the stop codon and the 30S head near bulged nucleotide C1054 of 16S rRNA.
evidence: This is observed in the RF2-bound structures.

claim: In Structure V, a 6° rotation of the 30S head shifts the position of C1054 by 5 Å from its position in RF2-bound Structure IV.
source: In Structure V, a 6° rotation of the 30S head shifts the position of C1054 by 5 Å from its position in RF2-bound Structure IV, consistent with disassembly of RF2 contacts.
evidence: This is measured by comparing Structures IV and V.

claim: The disruption of decoding-center interactions due to repositioning of H69 and head swivel explain the absence of RF2 in Structure V.
source: The disruption of decoding-center interactions due to repositioning of H69 and head swivel therefore explain the absence of RF2 in Structure V.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The termination structures allow reconstruction of a dynamic pathway for termination.
source: Our termination structures allow us to reconstruct a dynamic pathway for termination (Figure 4 and Animation 1) and reconcile biophysical and biochemical findings (Adio et al., 2018; Casy et al., 2018; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on the ensemble of structures obtained in this study.

claim: Recent structural studies revealed compact RF conformations on non-rotated 70S ribosomes that suggest how RFs open at early stages of codon recognition.
source: Recent structural studies revealed compact RF conformations on non-rotated 70S ribosomes (Fu et al., 2018; Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a) that suggest how RFs open at early stages of codon recognition (He and Green, 2010; Hetrick et al., 2009; Trappl and Joseph, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent structural and functional studies.

claim: The short-lived transition from compact to open conformation(s) of RF lasts tens of milliseconds.
source: The short-lived transition from compact to open conformation(s) lasts tens of milliseconds (Fu et al., 2018), and compact RF2 conformations were not captured in our sample.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2018.

claim: Compact RF2 conformations were not captured in the current sample.
source: The short-lived transition from compact to open conformation(s) lasts tens of milliseconds (Fu et al., 2018), and compact RF2 conformations were not captured in our sample.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current dataset.

claim: Compact RF2 was visualized by cryo-EM on the 70S ribosome in the presence of truncated mRNA and alternative rescue factor A (ArfA).
source: Compact RF2 was also visualized by cryo-EM on the 70S ribosome in the presence of truncated mRNA and alternative rescue factor A (ArfA) (Demo et al., 2017; James et al., 2016), suggesting a conserved pathway for initial binding of RFs to non-rotated ribosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Demo et al., 2017 and James et al., 2016.

claim: The observation of compact RF2 with ArfA suggests a conserved pathway for initial binding of RFs to non-rotated ribosomes.
source: Compact RF2 was also visualized by cryo-EM on the 70S ribosome in the presence of truncated mRNA and alternative rescue factor A (ArfA) (Demo et al., 2017; James et al., 2016), suggesting a conserved pathway for initial binding of RFs to non-rotated ribosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity observed in different contexts.

claim: The current work provides an expanded structural view of the termination reaction from initial codon recognition to peptide release to RF2 dissociation.
source: Together with these recent studies, our work provides an expanded structural view of the termination reaction – from initial codon recognition to peptide release to RF2 dissociation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary claim about the significance of the current work.

claim: Termination begins when release factor recognizes a stop codon in the A site of a non-rotated 70S ribosome carrying peptidyl-tRNA.
source: Termination begins when release factor recognizes a stop codon in the A site of a non-rotated (or slightly rotated) 70S ribosome carrying peptidyl-tRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge integrated into the termination model.

claim: A compact release factor recognizes the stop codon, while its catalytic domain is kept 60 to 70 Å away from the PTC.
source: A compact release factor recognizes the stop codon, while its catalytic domain is kept 60 to 70 Å away from the PTC (Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2018.

claim: Separation of the codon-recognition and catalytic functions during initial binding of RF underlies high accuracy of termination.
source: Separation of the codon-recognition and catalytic functions during initial binding of RF underlies high accuracy of termination (He and Green, 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008; Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a; Trappl and Joseph, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional and structural studies.

claim: Upon binding the decoding center, steric hindrance with P-tRNA forces the RF catalytic domain to undock from domain two and sample the intersubunit space.
source: Upon binding the decoding center, steric hindrance with P-tRNA forces the RF catalytic domain to undock from domain two and sample the intersubnit space (Figure 4B) (discussed in Svidritskiy and Korostelev, 2018a).
evidence: This is discussed in the cited reference and integrated into the model.

claim: The ribosome remains non-rotated because peptidyl-tRNA bridges the P sites of 30S and 50S subunits.
source: The ribosome remains non-rotated because peptidyl-tRNA bridges the P sites of 30S and 50S subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome dynamics.

claim: Interactions between the switch loop of RF and the decoding center and H69 direct the catalytic domain into the PTC.
source: Interactions between the switch loop of RF and the decoding center and H69 direct the catalytic domain into the PTC.
evidence: This is based on structural observations in the current and previous studies.

claim: The GGQ catalytic loop is placed next to the scissile ester bond of peptidyl-tRNA and stabilized by A2602.
source: The GGQ catalytic loop is placed next to the scissile ester bond of peptidyl-tRNA and stabilized by A2602 (Jin et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008), so that the Gln backbone amide of the GGQ motif can catalyze peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis (Figure 4C) (Korostelev et al., 2008; Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and mechanistic studies.

claim: The Gln backbone amide of the GGQ motif catalyzes peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis.
source: The GGQ catalytic loop is placed next to the scissile ester bond of peptidyl-tRNA and stabilized by A2602 (Jin et al., 2010; Laurberg et al., 2008), so that the Gln backbone amide of the GGQ motif can catalyze peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis (Figure 4C) (Korostelev et al., 2008; Santos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Korostelev et al., 2008 and Santos et al., 2013.

claim: Peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis is an irreversible step that separates the newly made protein from P-site tRNA and prevents further elongation.
source: These ribosome and RF2 rearrangements complete the first stage of termination leading to peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis—an irreversible step that separates the newly made protein from P-site tRNA and prevents further elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the termination mechanism.

claim: The deacylated CCA end of the tRNA exits the 50S P site, which allows movement of A2602.
source: The deacylated CCA end of the tRNA exits the 50S P site, which allows movement of A2602.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations in Structure II.

claim: No longer stabilized by the tRNA and A2602, the GGQ loop reorganizes into an extended β-hairpin that blocks the peptide tunnel.
source: No longer stabilized by the tRNA and A2602, the GGQ loop reorganizes into an extended β-hairpin that blocks the peptide tunnel (Structure II), thus biasing the diffusion of nascent peptide toward the exit of the peptide tunnel at the surface of the 50S subunit (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on the structural observation in Structure II and mechanistic inference.

claim: The β-hairpin biases the diffusion of nascent peptide toward the exit of the peptide tunnel at the surface of the 50S subunit.
source: No longer stabilized by the tRNA and A2602, the GGQ loop reorganizes into an extended β-hairpin that blocks the peptide tunnel (Structure II), thus biasing the diffusion of nascent peptide toward the exit of the peptide tunnel at the surface of the 50S subunit (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural observation that the β-hairpin plugs the tunnel.

claim: The exit of the CCA end from the P site supports formation of the P/E-tRNA hybrid conformation via spontaneous intersubunit rotation.
source: Furthermore, the exit of the CCA end from the P site supports formation of the P/E-tRNA hybrid conformation via spontaneous intersubunit rotation (Structures III and IV), which is also essential for translocation of tRNA-mRNA (reviewed in Ling and Ermolenko, 2016; Noller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the structural observations in Structures III and IV and supported by cited reviews.

claim: Spontaneous intersubunit rotation is essential for translocation of tRNA-mRNA.
source: Furthermore, the exit of the CCA end from the P site supports formation of the P/E-tRNA hybrid conformation via spontaneous intersubunit rotation (Structures III and IV), which is also essential for translocation of tRNA-mRNA (reviewed in Ling and Ermolenko, 2016; Noller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited reviews.

claim: The large counter-clockwise rotation of the small subunit destabilizes the catalytic domain of RF2.
source: The large counter-clockwise rotation of the small subunit destabilizes the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV), so that it begins to collapse toward domain 2 bound to the 30S subunit (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on the structural observation in Structure IV.

claim: The destabilized catalytic domain of RF2 begins to collapse toward domain 2 bound to the 30S subunit.
source: The large counter-clockwise rotation of the small subunit destabilizes the catalytic domain of RF2 (Structure IV), so that it begins to collapse toward domain 2 bound to the 30S subunit (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced density and comparison with free RF2 structure.

claim: Rotation of the 30S head and detachment of H69 from the decoding center force dissociation of RF2 from the A site of the 30S subunit.
source: Rotation of the 30S head and detachment of H69 from the decoding center force dissociation of RF2 from the A site of the 30S subunit (Structure V, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on the structural observations in Structure V.

claim: Similar extents of intersubunit rotation and head rotation were observed in recent RF1-bound 70S structures formed with RF3•GDPNP in the presence of apidaecin.
source: Remarkably similar extents of intersubunit rotation and head rotation were observed in recent RF1-bound 70S structures formed with RF3•GDPNP in the presence of apidaecin (which stalls RF1 on the ribosome).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the study by Graf et al., 2018.

claim: In the presence of stalled RF1, the intersubunit bridge remains attached to the decoding center.
source: In the presence of stalled RF1, however, the intersubunit bridge remains attached to the decoding center (Graf et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citation to Graf et al., 2018.

claim: The ribosome samples globally similar rotation states with RF1 and RF2, with or without RF3.
source: Thus, the ribosome samples globally similar rotation states with RF1 and RF2, with or without RF3.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the current structures with previous RF1 structures.

claim: RF3 stabilizes the rotated state to promote RF release.
source: RF3 stabilizes the rotated state (Ermolenko et al., 2007; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) to promote RF release.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of RF3 in termination is dispensable because intersubunit rotation is an inherent property of the ribosome.
source: However, the role of RF3 in termination is dispensable because intersubunit rotation is an inherent— that is spontaneous and thermally driven—property of the ribosome (Cornish et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cornish et al., 2008.

claim: Cold sensitivity of RF3-deletion strains perhaps manifests the dependence on RF3 due to perturbation of the intersubunit dynamics at lower temperatures.
source: Cold sensitivity of RF3-deletion strains (Nichols et al., 2011; O'Connor, 2015) perhaps manifests the dependence on RF3 due to perturbation of the intersubunit dynamics at lower temperatures.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cold sensitivity phenotype.

claim: In the fully rotated state, the post-termination ribosome becomes a substrate for subunit dissociation by EF-G and recycling factor RRF.
source: In the fully rotated state, the post-termination ribosome becomes a substrate for subunit dissociation by EF-G and recycling factor RRF (Agrawal et al., 2004; Dunkle et al., 2011; Fu et al., 2016; Prabhakar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Structure V is consistent with structural studies showing ribosome recycling factor (RRF) bound to ribosomes with a dislodged intersubunit bridge B2a.
source: Structure V is consistent with structural studies showing ribosome recycling factor (RRF) bound to ribosomes with a dislodged intersubunit bridge B2a (Borovinskaya et al., 2007; Pai et al., 2008), which helps split the ribosome into subunits.
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited structural studies of RRF-bound ribosomes.

claim: Dislodgement of bridge B2a helps split the ribosome into subunits.
source: Structure V is consistent with structural studies showing ribosome recycling factor (RRF) bound to ribosomes with a dislodged intersubunit bridge B2a (Borovinskaya et al., 2007; Pai et al., 2008), which helps split the ribosome into subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borovinskaya et al., 2007 and Pai et al., 2008.

claim: Translation termination and recycling of the release factors and the ribosome rely on the spontaneous ribosome dynamics.
source: Translation termination and recycling of the release factors and the ribosome therefore rely on the spontaneous ribosome dynamics (Adio et al., 2018; Cornish et al., 2008; Ermolenko et al., 2007; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009), coupled with local rearrangements of the universally conserved elements of the peptidyl-transferase and decoding centers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by multiple citations and the current structural data.

claim: Translation termination and recycling are coupled with local rearrangements of the universally conserved elements of the peptidyl-transferase and decoding centers.
source: Translation termination and recycling of the release factors and the ribosome therefore rely on the spontaneous ribosome dynamics (Adio et al., 2018; Cornish et al., 2008; Ermolenko et al., 2007; Prabhakar et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2009), coupled with local rearrangements of the universally conserved elements of the peptidyl-transferase and decoding centers.
evidence: This is based on the structural observations in the current study.
